intro: How do you learn about a religion that is not your own, or study your own with fresh eyes? Historians of religion have a toolkit. They read sacred texts as primary sources. They sort writings by genre, place events on a timeline and trace how traditions spread on a map. They also watch what people do: the rituals they repeat, the journeys they take and the buildings they raise.

This unit gives you that toolkit. In the first chapter you will read sources closely, learn what BCE, CE and c. mean, and see what a historian can and cannot say. In the second you will compare rites of passage, pilgrimages, houses of worship and holy days across many traditions, including ones you can visit in Chicago.

By the end, you will be able to describe a belief fairly by saying who holds it, read a text or a building for clues, and compare traditions without ranking them. These skills will guide every unit that follows.
bigQuestion: How can we study the world's religions fairly and accurately, through their texts, their times and their practices?

timeline.t: Composition of the Vedas, the oldest Hindu scriptures, begins
The Buddha teaches in northern India (dates vary)
Work begins on the Great Stupa at Sanchi in India
Paul writes letters to early Christian communities
Dionysius Exiguus counts years from the birth of Jesus
Muhammad moves to Medina; the Islamic calendar begins
Guru Nanak, first Sikh Guru, is born in Punjab
The World's Parliament of Religions meets in Chicago
The Bahá'í House of Worship in Wilmette, Illinois, is dedicated

words.d: something made by the people being studied, at or near the time
a later work that studies and explains primary sources
a kind of writing, such as law, story, poetry, prophecy or letter
the time, place and situation that surround a source
Latin for about; written c. before an estimated date
Before the Common Era and Common Era; the same years as BC and AD
saying who holds a belief, such as Hindus believe
an action done the same way on purpose, often with religious meaning
a ceremony marking a move to a new stage of life
a journey to a sacred place for religious reasons
a place a community sets apart as holy, such as a mosque or mandir
going without food or other things for a religious reason

test.q: A historian studies a hymn written by Guru Nanak. What kind of source is it?
test.why: The hymn comes from the founder of Sikhism himself.

test.q: Which genre is the book of Psalms?
test.why: The Psalms are 150 songs and prayers.

test.q: Which is earlier: 551 BCE or 479 BCE?
test.why: BCE years count down, so the larger number is earlier.

test.q: Which sentence is neutral and attributed?
choices: Jesus did not rise from the dead
Christianity is the largest, so it is right
Christians believe Jesus rose from the dead
test.why: Naming who holds the belief describes it without judging.

test.q: From which event does the Islamic calendar count?
choices: Muhammad's move to Medina in 622 CE
test.why: The Islamic calendar begins with the Hijra in 622 CE.

test.q: Which tradition has the most adherents today?
test.why: Common estimates put Christianity at about 2.4 billion.

test.why: A bat mitzvah marks a Jewish girl's coming of age.

test.q: Which pilgrimage place is sacred to Buddhists?
test.why: Buddhists believe the Buddha reached enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.

test.q: What does the mihrab in a mosque show?
choices: The place of the Torah scroll
test.why: The mihrab marks the qibla toward Mecca.

test.q: What stands at the center of a gurdwara's prayer hall?
test.why: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib on a raised seat.

test.q: How do pilgrims move at a stupa?
test.why: Buddhists walk clockwise around a stupa.

test.q: Which fast is kept by many Jews on the Day of Atonement?
test.why: Yom Kippur is the Jewish Day of Atonement.

test.q: What can a historian NOT decide with evidence?
choices: Whether a religious belief is true
test.why: Evidence shows beliefs and practices, not religious truth.

write.prompt: Pick two traditions from this unit. Using at least two sources or practices from the unit, such as a scripture verse, a holy day or a building, explain how each tradition marks sacred time or sacred space, and what that shows about what adherents value.
tips: Name each text, holiday or building you use.
Attribute every belief: write "Muslims believe" or "according to the Torah."
Compare the traditions; do not rank or judge them.
Use unit words such as ritual, pilgrimage and sacred space.
